title: I finally found a magnetic phone grip I never want to remove
teaser: The OhSnap Snap Grip Stand boasts a hinged arm that effortlessly props up your phone vertically—a massive upgrade over older magnet grips.
summary: This review details the OhSnap Snap Grip Stand, a magnetic accessory that finally meets the author's high standards. The thin (3.7mm) gadget features a double-sided magnetic ring and is built with durable bare anodized metal. Its standout feature is the hinged arm stand, which effortlessly props up the phone vertically—a significant improvement over rival grips like the Gornergrat Grat 5. The versatile grip can be used securely, offering multiple ways to hold the phone or attach it to surfaces like a fridge. While effective, the reviewer suggests improvements could include magnetizing the main ring for simultaneous use and lowering the price.
author: Sean Hollister
content: I told myself I wouldn't buy an OhSnap accessory for my phone. Every one I'd tested was nice, but felt overpriced and slightly flawed. After I weighed in on the $40 Snap Grip 5 last year, I wound up sticking with my $25 Syncwire instead. But OhSnap's $50 Snap Grip Stand finally got me. To have a truly useful vertical stand and grip always attached to my phone, ready at a moment's notice? Heck yes. I started testing the Snap Grip Stand months ago, and soon discovered that I never took it off . So I bought my own. It's thin - 3.7mm, so it slips effortlessly into my pocket without making an extra indent in my pants. It's got a double-sided magnetic ring, like the previous gen, so it not only sticks to your magnet ring phone, it can stick flat against a fridge or gym equipment or my garage cabinets. It even lets some wireless charging through. Like the previous gen, the magnets hold my phone tightly, and the grip part is one of the most versatile I've tried. The clever interlocking joints can fit between two of your fingers loosely like a PopSocket, or you can put a finger through the joints for a very secure grip. The whole disc spins freely (though still with a bit of scraping noise) to rotate to any angle you like. But unlike the previous gen, the Stand has a stand unlike most other magnet grips on the market. The entire magnet ring is now encircled by a thinner fold-out ring on a hinged arm. Pull it down, and it effortlessly props up my phone in its normal vertical orientation. Most rival stands barely prop a phone, and even then they don't deploy as fast. Here, there's no need to take off the stand, or rotate it and lock a tab in place like OhSnap's previous grips - pull out, plop phone on surface, done. OhSnap advertises that it's "thinner than your camera bumps," but that depends on whether you're using a case. It's thin enough. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge It's not the only stand with such a design. The $17 Gornergrat Grat 5 has a similar stand and costs far less. But I tried one and found I don't like its elastic strap, which feels loose and thus less secure around my fingers. OhSnap makes use of the extra vertical arm space to keep the stand from rotating when you don't want it to: it's got a extra vertical magnet in there to match Apple's MagSafe pattern, as well as some grippy clear plastic material to provide friction. And I'm happy to say the aluminum gadget doesn't seem to have any other unwanted coatings: I wasn't a fan of the adhesive on the Snap Grip 4, or the soft-touch coating that started to peel when I tested the Snap Grip 5. Here, it appears to be bare anodized metal that looks and feels great. Neither of these phones (Pixel 9, Galaxy S25) has built-in magnets, but I bought magnet cases for each. Phone grips like this also come with adhesive magnet rings. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge Right now, I can only think of three things that'd make it better: a lower price, magnets in the stand's ring (rather than the main ring) so I can use the magnets and the stand at the same time, and maybe a better way to open the grip one-handed. I do like how Tango's spring-loaded grip can pop open when you press it. But I tried a Tango too, and I don't like the way that spring feels between my fingers, pushing them apart too much. As for the lower price, at least OhSnap's products are regularly on sale. I bought mine at Best Buy for $40 after tax . title: Switched on Pop’s Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding love fresh vegetables and guitar pedals
teaser: Two music experts discuss analyzing pop perfection, sharing tips on tools like Sibelius notation software and the universal truth: you can never have too many guitar pedals.
summary: Music scholars Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding cohost 'Switched on Pop,' a popular podcast/Netflix series dedicated to dissecting the theory and production techniques behind pop songs. With near encyclopedic knowledge, they analyze everything from text painting in Justin Timberlake's work to obscure musicological details. During an interview, they highlighted their indispensable tools: Sloan relies on Sibelius for transcribing melodies, while Harding boasts about his extensive (and highly valued) collection of guitar pedals. The discussion also touched on daily tech woes, such as family group chat notifications disrupting focus, and shared anecdotes ranging from early tech pitches to pop culture critiques.
author: Terrence O’Brien
content: As if you needed more reason to love Carly Rae Jepsen's " Call Me Maybe " beyond its pop perfection, it is also, according to lore, the genesis for Switched on Pop , one of the best music podcasts out there. Cohosts Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding obsessively dissect pop songs, from the theory behind their musical choices to their production techniques. If you're a student of pop music, then this is a must-listen podcast. Sloan is a composer and professor of musicology at USC Thornton School of Music, where he researches pop, but also jazz and even Tin Pan Alley. Harding is a songwriter, music journalist, and a professor as well. Their combined knowledge is near encyclopedic. Whether they're talking about text painting in Justin Timberlake's "Can't Stop the Feeling!" or Taryn Southern's AI experiments, the two reveal the rich tapestry of even the most simple-seeming songs. Now, after 12 years and nearly 500 episodes, the show recently made the leap to video on Netflix, featuring guests like Aaron Dessner (The National), Trevor Horn (The Buggles, Yes), and Cypress Hill. Sloan and Harding told us about the importance of the metronome, fresh vegetables, and what seems to be a slightly problematic relationship with guitar pedals. Switched on Pop is a production of New York Magazine's Vulture and the Vox Media Podcast Network. What is your most indispensable tool? Charlie Harding: The Martin D-28 is the platonic idea of both what a guitar sounds like and, I'm ashamed to admit how much this matters to me, how a guitar looks. You've heard it on "Blackbird," "Wish You Were Here," and "Big Yellow Taxi." I found one from 1970 sitting in an antique shop in Maine. But I'm still waiting for it to produce a timeless classic for me. Nate Sloan: Sibelius music notation software. Whenever I'm analyzing a song, I don't truly understand it until I transcribe its melody, harmony, and rhythm. Which is the most underappreciated? CH: Keyboard shortcuts and the app Rectangle save me hours of my life every year by doing the mundane task of repositioning windows on my computer. And they also make me feel like I'm mission control on some kind of spaceship. What is the first app you install on a new phone or computer? NS: AudioHijack for grabbing audio. What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone? CH: This is very nitpicky, but it drives me mad. I extensively use focus modes on iOS to help keep away distractions. But I also need people in my family to be able to reach me, so they get exceptions to the focus modes. However, that means any group messaging chain with just one family member blows up my notifications when I'm presenting to a lecture hall full of songwriting students. This means I'm urgently notified every time my recently retired father catches a fish. I am happy for my dad, but I'd be more happy to find out after 5 pm when I'm off "do not disturb." If this makes me sound like a curmudgeon, I am. NS: I wish I could strum it like a guitar. What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar? NS: ProQuest Historical Newspapers. How many tabs do you have open right now? CH: 92... but they are nicely organized into groups that only I understand. NS: Two. I used to have hundreds open, but it was killing my attention span, so I now make a point of constantly closing them. Which social media platform do you use the most (if any)? What is your happy place online? CH: Browsing Sweetwater for variations of guitar pedals that I already own. NS: Watching ukulele tutorials on YouTube. What is your favorite gadget you've ever owned? CH: The Dato DUO synthesizer and Dato DRUM drum machine. They are the easiest way to learn to program a synthesizer, and you can't make a bad sound. My kids jam on them every night. It's turned them into Brooklyn DJs, unfortunately. NS: The iPod that I traveled around the world with in 2006. Which was the most disappointing? What game do you have the fondest memories of? Which tech trend do you wish would go away? CH: AI music slop, full stop. What is one thing you wish you had created? CH: In 2007 I pitched my college friends on creating an app that would allow you to legally hitchhike in other people's cars. We started a tea company instead, which was ultimately less of a liability. What creation are you most proud of? CH: Switched On Pop . My wife read this and said I should add my children. NS: Coining the term "pop drop" to describe the instrumental postchorus in a pop song. Which are you least proud of? CH: My wife read this and said I should say my guitar pedal collection. NS: Getting dunked on by YouTuber Rick Beato after calling the Jonas Brothers "stupefyingly funky" in a New York Times article. What's the best piece of advice you've ever received? CH: You can never have too many guitar pedals. What is your current obsession? NS: LeBron James signing with the 76ers. What do you do when you need to focus? NS: Step away from the computer, take a walk, and start recording a voicenote about what I'm trying to accomplish. What do you do when you're feeling stuck? NS: Call Charlie Harding. When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone? CH: During routine surgery. NS: Whenever I go to the gym. What's the last piece of physical media you bought? CH: The History of Sound by Ben Shattuck. NS: Vinyl copy of the Jeff Parker IVTet. What do you think is worth splurging on? CH: My guitar pedals. And my beautiful wife. What would the tagline for your biopic be? CH: He is embarrassed there is a biopic about him. NS: One man dared to overanalyze pop music, taking on BTS Army, Madonna stans, and the Little Monsters, and living to tell the tale. What's the last GIF or meme you used?
